study.title: Probability and random-variable notation
study.locator: Chapter 2, Sections 2.1 to 2.2 (pp. 33-38): events, the conditional-probability definition, discrete and continuous variables, CDFs and quantiles

focus: The naive definition needs finite and equally likely outcomes. State both assumptions before counting.
A PMF gives probabilities that sum to 1. A density does not: only its integral over a set is a probability, and a density value can exceed 1.
The CDF F(x) = P(X <= x) works for every variable type and determines the distribution.
Universality: for continuous X with CDF F, F(X) is Uniform(0,1). This is the seed of inverse-CDF sampling in the transforms unit.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, count P(sum of two fair dice = 9) = 4/36 = 1/9 from the 36 ordered pairs. Then check with NumPy in float64: numpy.random.default_rng(7), 200000 int64 pairs from integers(1, 7); the fraction of sums equal to 9 is 0.11259 with standard error 0.00071, within about 2 standard errors of 1/9.
traps: Reading a density value as a probability. For continuous X, P(X = x) = 0; report P(X in an interval) instead.
Calling an outcome random without a distribution. Name the set, the probabilities on it and the sampling scheme.
Assuming distinct-looking formulas give distinct distributions. Compare the CDF or the PMF values, which settle identity.

selfTest.q: Two dice: why is P(sum 9) = 4/36 and not 4/11?
selfTest.a: Sums 2 to 12 are 11 values but not equally likely, so the naive definition does not apply to them. The 36 ordered pairs are equally likely by symmetry of fair independent dice, and 4 of them sum to 9. The step that uses the assumption is choosing the 36 pairs as the counting set.

selfTest.q: Give a density that exceeds 1 somewhere and show it is still valid.
selfTest.a: Uniform(0, 0.5) has density 2 on its support and integrates to 1. Validity uses non-negativity plus integral 1; no step bounds the density pointwise.

selfTest.q: X is continuous with strictly increasing CDF F. Prove F(X) is Uniform(0,1), naming each assumption.
selfTest.a: P(F(X) <= u) = P(X <= F^{-1}(u)) uses strict increase for the inverse step, then equals F(F^{-1}(u)) = u by continuity of F. The result u on (0,1) is the Uniform CDF.

selfTest.q: A learner simulates 2000 dice pairs, gets 0.125, and claims the exact answer is wrong. What is the error?
selfTest.a: Simulation noise. The standard error is about sqrt((1/9)(8/9)/2000) = 0.0079, so 0.125 is within 2 standard errors of 1/9. A simulation reports an estimate with its standard error; it never refutes an exact count.

study.title: Chain rule and conditional independence
study.locator: Chapter 2, Sections 2.1.3.4-2.1.3.6 and 2.2.3-2.2.4 (pp. 35, 38-40): conditional probability, product and chain rules, independence and conditional independence

focus: P(A|B) = P(A,B)/P(B) restricts the sample space to B. Write the restricted space before computing.
The chain rule factors any joint distribution. An independence claim drops a conditioning bar and must be justified, never assumed silently.
Conditioning can reverse a comparison, as Simpson examples show. Report the conditioning set with every rate.
Monty Hall rewards writing the host protocol as a conditional distribution, not as unconditional door odds.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, derive P(both boys | at least one boy) = 1/3: the reduced space {BB, BG, GB} is equally likely and one outcome in three is BB. Check with NumPy in float64: numpy.random.default_rng(11), 300000 pairs from integers(0, 2); the conditional fraction is 0.33357 over 225364 conditioned pairs, with standard error 0.00099.
traps: Swapping P(A|B) with P(B|A). Write both conditionals with their different denominators.
Reading pairwise independence as mutual independence. A three-coin Bernstein-style construction breaks it by hand.
Confusing conditional with marginal independence in either direction. The skill-level examples in Strategic Practice 2 separate the two.

selfTest.q: Derive Bayes rule from the definition of conditional probability and name the step that needs P(B) > 0.
selfTest.a: P(A|B) = P(A,B)/P(B) and P(B|A) = P(A,B)/P(A); eliminating P(A,B) gives P(A|B) = P(B|A)P(A)/P(B). Division needs P(B) > 0, and expanding P(B) by total probability needs a partition of the space.

selfTest.q: Two fair coins. Are {first is heads} and {at least one head} independent?
selfTest.a: No. P(first H) = 1/2 and P(at least one H) = 3/4, but the joint event {HH} has probability 1/4, which differs from the product 3/8.

selfTest.q: Give variables that are conditionally independent given Z but marginally dependent.
selfTest.a: Two symptoms given disease status: given Z they are independent by the modeling assumption, but unconditionally they correlate through the unobserved common cause Z.

selfTest.q: In Reproduce, why is the answer 1/3 and not 1/2?
selfTest.a: Conditioning on at least one boy leaves {BB, BG, GB}, three equally likely outcomes. The 1/2 answer conditions on a different event, namely that a specified child is a boy.

study.title: Moments and the total laws
study.locator: Chapter 2, Section 2.2.5 (pp. 40-43): mean, linearity, variance, law of total expectation and law of total variance with the mixture example

focus: Linearity of expectation needs no independence. The variance of a sum needs uncorrelatedness; independence is sufficient, not necessary.
Eve's law splits variance into explained plus residual: Var(Y) = Var(E[Y|X]) + E[Var(Y|X)]. Name which term each modeling choice changes.
Taking out what is known, E[g(X)Y|X] = g(X)E[Y|X], needs g(X) fixed given X. Conditioning on the wrong variable breaks it.
Zero correlation with clear dependence is one construction away: take X symmetric about 0 and Y = X^2, then Cov(X,Y) = 0 by symmetry.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, derive Eve's law on a two-stage model: with probability 1/2 roll a fair die (mean 3.5, variance 35/12) and otherwise take 10. Then E[X] = 6.75 and Var(X) = 35/24 + (10 - 3.5)^2/4 = 12.0208: the first term uses LOTUS on the die branch and the second uses Var of {3.5, 10}. Check with NumPy in float64: numpy.random.default_rng(21), 400000 draws; sample mean 6.7493 and variance 12.023 with standard error of the mean 0.00548.
traps: Pushing a nonlinear function inside an expectation. E[g(X)] differs from g(E[X]); Jensen fixes the direction for convex g.
Dropping the covariance term in Var(X + Y) without checking uncorrelatedness first.
Quoting a conditional expectation as a number. E[Y|X] is a function of X; only E[Y|X = x] is a number.

selfTest.q: Prove Eve's law from the definition of variance, naming where each assumption is used.
selfTest.a: Write Var(Y) = E[Y^2] - E[Y]^2, then condition: E[Y^2] = E[E[Y^2|X]] by Adam's law, which needs E|Y^2| finite. Subtract E[E[Y|X]]^2 after writing E[Y] = E[E[Y|X]] by the same law, and regroup into E[Var(Y|X)] + Var(E[Y|X]). Both steps use iterated expectation, hence integrability.

selfTest.q: X is symmetric about 0 with E|X|^3 finite and Y = X^2. Show Cov(X, Y) = 0 while X and Y are dependent.
selfTest.a: E[XY] = E[X^3] = 0 by symmetry, and E[X] = 0, so Cov = 0 - 0 = 0. Dependence holds because |X| = sqrt(Y): knowing Y pins down |X|.

selfTest.q: In Reproduce, which part of 12.0208 comes from within-branch variation and which from between-branch variation?
selfTest.a: 35/24 = 1.4583 is E[Var(X|branch)], the within part, all of it from the die since the constant branch has zero variance. (10 - 3.5)^2/4 = 10.5625 is Var(E[X|branch]), the between part.

selfTest.q: Why does the reproduce check quote 0.00548 alongside the mean?
selfTest.a: It is the simulation standard error, sd/sqrt(n). Without it the comparison of 6.7493 against 6.75 has no scale; agreement means within a few standard errors.

study.title: Distribution families and change of variables
study.locator: Chapter 2, Sections 2.4-2.6 (pp. 49-57) for Bernoulli, categorical and Gaussian; Section 2.8.3-2.8.5 (pp. 67-71) for bijections, the Jacobian factor and convolutions

focus: Tie each family to a sampling story: counts of trials, waiting times, arrivals per interval. The story selects the family; the data never does by itself.
A change of variables multiplies by the Jacobian absolute determinant and re-derives the support. A density without a support is unfinished.
Sums of independent variables convolve densities; MGFs turn convolution into multiplication where the MGF exists near zero.
Parametrization traps: Exponential and Gamma rate versus scale, Normal variance versus standard deviation. State yours in every signature.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, derive by the CDF method that U ~ Uniform(0,1) gives X = -log(U) ~ Expo(1): P(X <= x) = P(U >= e^-x) = 1 - e^-x for x >= 0, using continuity of U for the strict-inequality step. Then check with NumPy in float64: numpy.random.default_rng(31), 300000 draws via random() then -log; sample mean 0.9983 and variance 1.0024 against exact 1 and 1, and P(X > 2) = 0.1341 against exact e^-2 = 0.1353 with standard error 0.00062.
traps: Dropping the Jacobian factor or keeping the old support after a transform. Both silently produce a function that does not integrate to 1.
Assuming every distribution has an MGF. Cauchy has none; quote the MGF only with its domain.
Confusing Poisson counts with Exponential waiting times. They describe one process from two sides; the units differ.

selfTest.q: Derive the density of Y = X^2 for X ~ Uniform(-1, 1), naming the non-monotone step.
selfTest.a: F_Y(y) = P(-sqrt(y) <= X <= sqrt(y)) = sqrt(y) on (0,1), using the two-sided preimage; differentiating gives f_Y(y) = 1/(2 sqrt(y)) on (0,1). The monotone CDF rule applied to one branch alone would halve the answer.

selfTest.q: Why does Box-Muller produce two independent Normals from two Uniforms?
selfTest.a: The polar map (U1, U2) -> (R cos, R sin) with R^2 = -2 log U1 has Jacobian factor that splits the joint density into a product of two standard Normal densities. Independence is read off the factored form.

selfTest.q: X ~ Pois(2) counts arrivals per hour and T ~ Expo(2) is the wait for the next arrival. Are X and T the same object?
selfTest.a: No. X is discrete with mean 2; T is continuous with mean 1/2 hour. Same rate parameter, different sample spaces and different questions.

selfTest.q: In Reproduce, why is random() with -log enough, and what would break with integers(0, 2)?
selfTest.a: Inverse-CDF needs a continuous Uniform(0,1) input so that P(U >= u) = 1 - u; the proof step uses continuity. A discrete input would quantize X and the CDF derivation would fail.

study.title: Beta-Binomial posterior and posterior predictive
study.locator: Chapter 4, Sections 4.6.1-4.6.2.9 (pp. 129-135): conjugate priors, Beta-Binomial posterior, MAP, posterior predictive and marginal likelihood
study.depth: Stop before Section 4.6.8. Laplace, variational and MCMC computation belong to later stages.

focus: Conjugacy is algebra: a Beta prior times a Binomial likelihood is Beta up to a constant. The update adds successes to a and failures to b.
The posterior predictive averages over the posterior; the plug-in forecast conditions on one estimate. They differ most with little data.
The evidence normalizes the posterior for fixed data and compares models across hypotheses. It never rescales a single posterior's shape.
A graphical factorization is a chain-rule product with dropped conditioning bars. Each dropped bar is a conditional-independence claim to defend.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, derive the Beta-Binomial update for a Beta(2, 2) prior with 7 heads in 10 flips: posterior Beta(9, 5), mean 9/14 = 0.6429, MAP 8/12 = 0.6667, posterior predictive P(next head) = 9/14. Check with NumPy in float64: numpy.random.default_rng(41), 300000 beta(9, 5) draws; posterior mean 0.6430 with standard error 0.00023, one binomial flip per draw gives predictive fraction 0.6439, and the 2.5 and 97.5 percent quantiles give the 95 percent credible interval [0.385, 0.862].
traps: Reporting the MAP as the posterior mean. They coincide only for symmetric posteriors; here 0.6667 differs from 0.6429.
Reading a 95 percent credible interval as a 95 percent confidence interval. One conditions on the observed data with a prior; the other is a pre-data coverage statement.
Reusing the same data to pick the prior and to update. That double counts the evidence; run a prior-sensitivity check instead.

selfTest.q: Derive the Beta(9, 5) posterior from Bayes rule and name the step that uses conjugacy.
selfTest.a: Posterior is proportional to theta^7(1-theta)^3 times theta^1(1-theta)^1 = theta^8(1-theta)^4. Recognizing this kernel as Beta(9, 5) up to its normalizing constant is the conjugacy step; it uses the Beta integral identity.

selfTest.q: Derive the posterior predictive 9/14 and state the assumption that lets the integral close.
selfTest.a: P(next head | data) = integral of theta times Beta(9, 5) = E[theta] = 9/14. The integral closes because the Bernoulli likelihood is linear in theta and the posterior is Beta; exchangeability of the flips justifies reusing the same theta.

selfTest.q: How does the predictive probability move if the prior changes from Beta(2, 2) to Beta(20, 20) with the same 7-in-10 data?
selfTest.a: Posterior becomes Beta(27, 33) with mean 27/60 = 0.45, pulled from 0.6429 toward the prior mean 0.5. Sensitivity shrinks as data grow: the prior contributes a fixed pseudo-count against n real trials.

selfTest.q: A two-node graph X -> Y claims p(x, y) = p(x)p(y|x). What does the missing bar encode?
selfTest.a: Nothing is dropped here: it is the chain rule. A claim appears only with more parents or missing edges, for example p(y|x, z) = p(y|x), which asserts Y is independent of Z given X.
